title: Chemical spill in the lab
summary: A bottle of acid smashes on the bench and splashes your partner's eye. Raise the alarm, rinse, gear up and contain the spill.
sources: CLEAPSS Student Safety Sheets and school laboratory guidance
Standard school lab first aid: flush eyes with running water for at least 15 minutes

scenes.narration: Crash! A bottle of dilute sulfuric acid slips off the shelf and smashes. Acid spreads over the bench, and your lab partner cries out: some splashed in her eye.

hints.text: Someone is hurt and there's acid everywhere. Who in the room is in charge and needs to know right now?
Look at the door: your teacher is there.
Use your hands on your teacher: shout "Acid spill, and it's in her eye!"

choices.label: Shout for the teacher: "Acid spill, and it's in her eye!"
choices.feedback: Yes. A spill with a casualty: the teacher must know straight away, and saying what it is helps them act fast.

choices.label: It's only dilute. Keep working.
choices.feedback: Even dilute acid damages eyes and irritates skin, and a spill spreads. It needs dealing with now.

scenes.narration: Your partner is holding her eye and it's stinging badly. The teacher is on the way. The eyewash station is on the far wall.

hints.text: Acid keeps burning until it's washed away. What washes an eye properly, and for how long?
Look at the far wall: there's a station made just for eyes.
Use your hands on the eyewash station: lead her there and flush her eye for at least 15 minutes, eyelid held open.

choices.label: Lead her to the eyewash and flush the eye for at least 15 minutes, eyelid held open
choices.feedback: Right. Flush a chemical splash in the eye with gently running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, even after it stops stinging.

choices.label: Splash a little water from the sink in her eye
choices.feedback: A quick splash isn't enough. The eye needs a steady flow for at least 15 minutes. Use the eyewash station.

choices.label: Dab some neutraliser on her eye
choices.feedback: Never put any chemical in an eye or on skin. Water only, and lots of it.

choices.label: Tell her to rub her eye
choices.feedback: Rubbing grinds the acid in. Hold the eye open under running water instead.

scenes.narration: Your partner is flushing her eye at the eyewash. Your teacher, at the door, checks on her and asks you to deal with the spill with the spill kit, as you've practised. Acid is creeping towards the edge of the bench.

hints.text: Before you touch any chemical, what protects you?
Look at yourself: are your eyes and hands protected?
Use "Goggles + gloves" on You before touching anything.

choices.label: Put on goggles and chemical-resistant gloves first
choices.feedback: Yes. Protect your eyes and hands before you go near a spill. That's how you avoid becoming the next casualty.

choices.label: Grab paper towels and mop it up bare-handed
choices.feedback: Never handle a chemical spill with bare hands or without goggles. Gear up first, then use the spill kit.

choices.label: Pick up the broken glass first
choices.feedback: Acid-covered glass can cut and burn you. Gear up, and use a dustpan and brush, never fingers.

scenes.narration: Goggles and gloves on. The acid is about to drip off the bench onto the floor.

hints.text: The spill is spreading. Would you stop a puddle by adding more liquid, or by building a wall around it?
Look at the acid spill, and work from the outside edge in.
Use the spill kit absorbent on the acid spill to ring it in.

choices.label: Ring the spill with absorbent from the spill kit, working from the outside in
choices.feedback: Right. Surround the spill first so it can't spread, then cover it, working from the edges inward.

choices.label: Wash it away with a bucket of water
choices.feedback: Flooding spreads the acid over a bigger area and onto the floor. Contain it first with the spill kit.

choices.label: Soak it up with paper towels
choices.feedback: Paper towels fall apart and drip. The spill kit's absorbent is made for this. Ring the spill first.

scenes.narration: The spill is ringed in. Your teacher calls over: "Neutralise it as we practised."

hints.text: An acid is neutralised by a base, but a gentle one. A strong alkali reacts violently and burns skin too.
Use the neutraliser (sodium hydrogencarbonate) on the spill until the fizzing stops.

choices.label: Sprinkle sodium hydrogencarbonate over it until the fizzing stops
choices.feedback: Yes. A mild neutraliser from the spill kit, added slowly, makes acid safe to clear. Fizzing (carbon dioxide) stopping means it's done.

choices.label: Pour sodium hydroxide on it to neutralise it faster
choices.feedback: Strong alkali reacts violently with acid, getting hot and spattering, and is corrosive itself. Use the mild neutraliser from the kit.

choices.label: Pick the glass out with your gloved fingers
choices.feedback: Glass cuts through gloves. Neutralise first, then sweep glass up with a dustpan and brush into the broken-glass bin.

scenes.narration: The fizzing has stopped. Your partner is still flushing her eye at the eyewash.

hints.text: Someone was injured. Who needs the full story so she gets checked and it's written up?
Use your hands on your teacher: say what spilled, roughly how much, and that it went in her eye.

choices.label: Tell the teacher what spilled, roughly how much, and that it went in her eye
choices.feedback: Good. Clear information helps the teacher decide on medical care (any chemical in the eye needs checking by a doctor) and record the incident.

choices.label: Scoop the waste into the sink and go back to your experiment
choices.feedback: Spill waste goes in a labelled bag for the teacher to dispose of, and the teacher needs to know exactly what happened.

end-safe.text: Your partner's eye is flushed for 15 minutes and she goes to the doctor to have it checked. The spill is cleared, bagged and labelled. Calm, quick action made the difference.

end-unsafe.text: The spill spread and more people were splashed.

learn: Tell the teacher immediately about any spill or splash, and say what it is.
Chemical in the eye: eyewash, eyelid held open, at least 15 minutes, then see a doctor. Never put another chemical on skin or eyes.
Goggles and gloves on before going near a spill.
Contain the spill with the spill kit from the outside in, then neutralise it with the mild neutraliser as your teacher instructs.
Never pick up broken glass with your fingers; use a dustpan and brush.
disclaimer: Training only. This is not a substitute for emergency services or certified first-aid and fire-safety training. In a real emergency in India, call 112.
